article_notes: Prospective study of 75 dogs with B. rossi (smear, PCR-RLB) admitted to the OVAH ICU; 68 analysed (11 died, 57 survived; 1 euthanased for other reasons excluded). Dogs euthanased for reasons other than poor prognosis were excluded, which implies dogs euthanased for poor prognosis were counted as non-survivors. Admission serum taken before any therapy; daily samples thereafter. CRP unit is printed as 'mg/ ' (the litre glyph was lost in PDF conversion; mg/L). Figure 2 caption gives P = 0.64 for the CRP vs hospitalisation regression whereas the Results text and abstract give P = 0.65.

severity_definitions.label: non-survivors vs survivors
severity_definitions.definition: Died (including euthanasia for poor prognosis) vs survived and discharged.
severity_definitions.quote: Outcome was recorded as the patient survived and was discharged or died.

severity_definitions.label: length of ICU stay (days hospitalised) in survivors
severity_definitions.definition: Number of days of hospitalisation in the ICU among survivors (continuous); longer stay taken as more severe.
severity_definitions.quote: Among survivors, multiple regression analysis was used to examine the relationship between CRP concentration at admission and length of stay in ICU, adjusting for age and sex.

associations.statistic: mean ± SD 122.1 ± 64.6 vs 107.5 ± 49.5 mg/L; exact logistic regression adjusted for age and sex
associations.quote: There was no significant difference in mean CRP concentration between survivors ( n = 57), 107.5 ± 49.5 mg/ and non-survivors ( n = 11), 122.1 ± 64.6 mg/ at admission and using the exact logistic regression, adjusting for age and sex, there was no association with outcome ( P = 0.53).
associations.note: The only test of CRP against outcome is the exact logistic regression; the group means are descriptive.

associations.statistic: survival 100 % (9/9) with CRP <60 vs 81.4 % (48/59) with CRP >=60; Fisher's exact test; cut-off chosen retrospectively
associations.quote: the survival rate for dogs with an admission CRP concentration <60 mg/ was 100 % (9/9) and those dogs with an admission CRP concentration ≥ 60 mg/ was 81.4 % (48/59). However, these 2 proportions did not differ significantly using a Fisher’s exact test ( P = 0.34).
associations.note: Proportions are survival per CRP group, not CRP category per outcome group, so severe_value and comparison_value are null. No non-survivor had admission CRP below 63.2 mg/L.

associations.statistic: multiple regression of days in ICU on admission CRP, adjusted for age and sex
associations.quote: the multiple regression analysis failed to show a significant relationship between these 2 variables, adjusting for age and sex ( P = 0.65)
associations.note: Figure 2 caption gives P = 0.64 for the same analysis; the authors describe an apparent but non-significant positive relationship.

associations.marker_as_reported: magnitude of change in CRP over the first 24 hours
associations.statistic: multiple linear regression of days in ICU on 24-h CRP change, adjusted for age and sex
associations.quote: there was no significant association between the magnitude of change in CRP concentration over the 1st 24 hours from admission and the number of days of hospitalisation ( P = 0.34)
associations.note: Adjustment for age and sex stated in Methods.

associations.statistic: median days hospitalised 2 (range 1-6; n=48) with CRP >=60 vs 3 (range 2-4; n=9) with CRP <60; Wilcoxon rank-sum
associations.quote: There was also no significant difference in the median number of days hospitalised in those dogs that survived with an admission CRP concentration <60 mg/ (3 days, range 2–4 days; n = 9) compared with those survivors with an admission CRP concentration ≥ 60 mg/ (2 days, range 1–6 days; n = 48), using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test ( P = 0.25).
associations.note: Groups defined by the CRP cut-off; the outcome (days hospitalised) is compared. The median stay was shorter in the high-CRP group (non-significant), hence negative_association.
